summary: Our app uses SAR data to detect floods, earthquakes, fires, volcanic eruptions, and landslides. It helps researchers understand hazard patterns and helps communities prepare, which protects farms, improves yields, and strengthens local economies
details:
Dancing with the SARs: press play on a season of radar

What it does. A web app that lets anyone watch the Earth's surface change through NISAR, the NASA and ISRO radar satellite. Pick a place on the globe, press play, and see one season of radar passes (June to October 2026), with a plain-language explanation of what is happening and why radar can see it. It covers 37 places on five continents: floods, lakes, wetlands, farmland, wildfires, earthquakes, volcanoes, a landslide and a storm.

How it works. A Python pipeline downloads NISAR data from NASA's Alaska Satellite Facility, aligns the passes, detects change and exports small images to a static web app. Detection is mathematics on PyTorch tensors: speckle filtering, a terrain mask, a change-point test that dates each pixel's change, and a probability-based water detector. Earthquakes use interferometry to measure ground displacement before and after an event.

Benefits and impact. Radar sees through cloud, smoke and darkness, so floods and fires are visible when optical satellites are blind. We turn complex SAR data into something students, journalists and local decision makers can read in a minute, and every layer carries a caution label so maps are not over-read.

Tools. Python, PyTorch, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, h5py, asf_search, earthaccess, pytest (243 tests); JavaScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL; NASA GIBS, NASA POWER, SRTM, OPERA and Landsat for comparison; Git and GitHub; team laptops and one small cloud server.

Creativity. A season of radar plays like a film, with a map of when each pixel changed. We show failures on purpose: a lake that does not change but fools a naive method, and a valley where fields are smaller than a pixel. A "How we found it" stepper explains the method for each kind of place.

Factors considered. Honesty (we compared our maps with Landsat and NASA's OPERA product and publish where ours are wrong), the limits of one season with an instrument gap from 27 July to 10 August, pixel resolution, fast loading on slow connections with no login, and low cost.
